summary: An April Fools' RFC that jokingly proposes to boost IPv6 by turning social networking platforms into IPv6 networks, instantly adding millions of hosts. It is humor and not a real protocol.

eli5.summary: Not many computers used the new internet addressing, so this joke suggests simply counting everyone on social networks as using it. It is only a silly idea for April 1st.

questions: what is ipv6 over social networks
how does ipv6 over facebook work
subtitle: A humorous April Fools proposal to fix IPv6 adoption.

tldr.problem: IPv6 adoption was still very low in early 2009, despite being a standard for years. Network engineers wanted more IPv6 nodes on the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' RFC jokingly proposes treating social networks as IPv6 networks: each user becomes a router, each friendship becomes a link, and every user's account gets an IPv6 address.
tldr.outcome: The author actually built a working prototype on Facebook to demonstrate the concept. Packets travel between users as they manually invoke the IPv6 processing, creating extremely high latencies (multi-day ping times).

today: RFC 5514 is a humor document from April Fools' Day 2009. It is not a real protocol and was never intended for deployment. However, it demonstrates an interesting property of delay-tolerant networks and remains a beloved example of IETF humor. The Facebook prototype has long since disappeared.

sections.title: The Joke
sections.content:
RFC 5514, published on April 1, 2009, is a humorous proposal to solve the slow adoption of IPv6. The idea is absurdly simple: turn every social network into an IPv6 network. Each user becomes an IPv6 router with a loopback interface, and each friendship link between users becomes a point-to-point network link. This would instantly add millions of IPv6 hosts to the Internet.

The RFC is tongue-in-cheek but technically coherent, describing actual architecture, addressing schemes, and routing protocol choices.
sections.eli5: The joke: Everyone on Facebook is already your friend, so why not count them as part of the IPv6 internet? It is silly but the author actually built it.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
In IPoSN (IPv6 over Social Networks), each user's social network account is assigned an IPv6 address derived from their unique user ID. The global unicast address uses a /64 prefix (such as 2001:db8:face:b00c::/64) followed by the user's ID; link-local addresses use fe80::/64 with the same user ID appended.

Packets only propagate when a user manually activates the IPoSN application on their account. This creates extraordinarily high latency—the proposal recommends RIPng routing because traditional OSPF cannot tolerate delays measured in hours or days. UDP should be used; TCP will not work.
sections.eli5: Each person gets an IPv6 address based on their Facebook ID. Messages hop from friend to friend, but only when each person manually clicks a button. A ping might take days.

sections.title: The Prototype
sections.content:
Remarkably, the author built a real working prototype on Facebook. In March 2009, it had 3,800 nodes and was routing IPv6 packets across the social graph. The statistics include actual ping and traceroute outputs showing latencies spanning days: a ping request sent February 24 received a reply February 26; a traceroute that started February 25 reached its destination March 1.

The application processed about 160 packets per minute and demonstrated the principle works, albeit slowly. The joke has become a real proof of concept.
sections.eli5: The author actually made this work on Facebook. When you pinged someone, it took 2 days to get a response. The longer the chain of friends, the longer the wait.
